The repository has Cargo/npm dependency manifests and lockfiles, five GitHub Actions workflows including a release/publish path, and an installer that downloads and executes a released binary.

findings.title: Release tags are neither cryptographically signed nor protected by a repository ruleset

evidence.source: manual read of release.yml's tag-validation step
evidence.note: The 'Validate release tag and package version' step only regex-matches the tag name against ^v(...)$ and cross-checks it equals the Cargo.toml package version. It never calls `git tag -v` or checks any cryptographic signature before the rest of the release pipeline (build, self-scan, package, attest, publish) runs.

rulesets returns an empty array `[]`; tags/protection returns 404 Not Found. No branch or tag protection ruleset exists on this repository, so any collaborator or leaked token with push access can create and push an arbitrary `v*` tag.

findings.problem: The only gate on what becomes a `vX.Y.Z` release tag is the regex-and-version-match step inside release.yml itself, which runs *after* the tag already exists and *after* GitHub Actions has already started a workflow run in response to it. There is no tag protection ruleset restricting who can push matching tags, and no signature requirement (`git tag -s` / `git tag -v`) anywhere in the release process or documented as a runbook step.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who obtains push access to the repository (a compromised maintainer token, an overly-broad CI token, or a maintainer account takeover) pushes a `vX.Y.Z` tag pointing at a malicious commit. Nothing at the tag layer stops this: release.yml's own checks only validate the tag *string* against the package version, not who pushed it or whether it is signed. The build-provenance attestation (verified working end-to-end against the real v0.7.0-beta.6 release assets during this audit) would still correctly attest that *this repository's workflow* built the resulting ZIPs -- but it would attest to the malicious commit just as faithfully as a legitimate one, because attestation proves build provenance, not tag authenticity.
findings.minimal_fix: Add a GitHub ruleset restricting tag creation matching `v*` to designated release actors (or requiring a signed commit/tag), closing the gap issue #158 explicitly calls out. This is a repository-settings change, not a code change.
findings.long_term_fix: Adopt `git tag -s` for release tags with the signing key and process documented in a maintainer runbook (docs/release-provenance-runbook.md, added alongside this audit), and consider verifying the tag signature as an explicit release.yml step before the release-windows job starts, so an unsigned tag fails closed instead of silently proceeding.
findings.regression_test: Not applicable as an automated regression test today -- this is a repository-configuration gap, not a code path. The closest verifiable regression test is a documented, repeatable manual check: `gh api repos/2233admin/code-intel-pipeline/rulesets` returns a non-empty ruleset covering tag refs matching `v*`.

Not assessed: this run was intentionally scoped to the supply-chain department per issue #158.

One confirmed, isolated medium-severity finding (unsigned/unprotected release tags) with a clear, local fix. Every other inspected control held: all five GitHub Actions workflows pin every third-party action by full commit SHA, use least-privilege `permissions:` blocks (contents: read by default, escalated only in release.yml's publish job), and use no `pull_request_target`; every Cargo and npm dependency resolves through a committed lockfile with no git/branch-pinned sources; the release ZIP's GitHub Artifact Attestation was independently downloaded and verified end-to-end against the real, already-published v0.7.0-beta.6 assets for all three platforms during this audit (`gh attestation verify`, exit 0, valid Sigstore certificate chain to release.yml@refs/tags/v0.7.0-beta.6); and the Skill install path (bootstrap.py) now verifies that same attestation before trusting a download, degrading explicitly (not silently) when `gh` is unavailable.
